query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating high‐throughput DSC with in situ synchrotron XRD measurements and validating the results via atomistic free‐energy integration from ab initio molecular dynamics will accurately quantify melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting for high‐entropy alloys with error margins around ±5% compared to benchmarks from simpler systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic or near‐equiatomic high‐entropy alloy samples prepared as single-phase solid solutions.
generation.intervention: Application of high‐throughput DSC combined with in situ synchrotron XRD during controlled heating cycles, followed by free‐energy integration through ab initio MD simulations.
generation.conditions: High temperature heating near the melting point under near‐equilibrium conditions, across a representative range of HEA compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time phase evolution as observed by in situ XRD, capturing transitions from ordered solid to disordered liquid phases.
generation.mechanism: DSC detects latent heat release while XRD tracks crystallographic changes at melting; subsequent AIMD free‐energy integration links these thermal events to quantitative fusion enthalpy, entropy, and volume change, allowing cross-validation of the thermodynamic parameters.
generation.predicted_outcome: Consistent extraction of melting properties (melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change) with quantifiable accuracy (approximately ±5% deviation) across various HEA compositions, with DSC peaks correlating with XRD-detected phase transitions and supported by simulation data.
generation.baseline: Traditional calorimetric methods and static XRD analyses that work well for binary or ternary alloys but are less efficient or precise for HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be limited to HEAs that form single-phase solid solutions and may not perform well in cases of severe phase segregation or extreme kinetic impediments during rapid heating.
generation.uncertainty: The method's scalability across the full compositional range of HEAs and its reproducibility under varied kinetic conditions remain uncertain until further systematic validation is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of HEA samples covering a broad compositional range. Subject each sample to a controlled heating schedule while simultaneously recording DSC and in situ XRD data. Perform independent ab initio MD free‐energy integration for the same compositions. Compare the melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, entropies, and volume changes derived from both experimental and computational methods.
measurements: DSC-derived onset temperatures and latent heat values
XRD-determined phase transition points and structural evolution data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fusion properties obtained from the integrated DSC/XRD method and AIMD free‐energy integration deviate by more than ±5% from each other or from accepted values in simpler alloy systems, or if the DSC peaks and XRD phase-transition events do not correlate, then the proposed method would be ruled out as an accurate and efficient approach for determining HEA melting properties.

cited_evidence.text: We study the effects of the chemical short-range order (SRO) on the thermal conductivity of the refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr using atomistic simulation. Samples with different degrees of chemical SRO are prepared by a Monte Carlo scheme. With increasing SRO, a tendency of forming HfTi and TiZr clusters is found. The phonon density of states is determined from the velocity auto-correlation function and chemical SRO modifies the high-frequency part of the phonon density of states. Lattice heat conductivity is calculated by non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. The heat conductivity of the random alloy is lower than that of the segregated binary alloys. Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce scattering times and, therefore, decrease thermal conductivity. We find that, in contrast, due to the increase of the conductivity alongside SRO cluster percolation pathways, SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12 %. This is expected to be a general result, extending to other HEAs.

Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems. To extend the potential of nanoalloys in different fields such as catalysis or mechanics, much attention has recently been paid to multi‐element nanoparticles (NPs), also known as high‐entropy nanoalloys (HENA), which consist of nanostructures composed of five or more metals, in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized in a solid solution. [ [1] ] Although many physical and chemical fabrication methods have been developed [ [2] ] there are still many gray areas concerning the synthesis‐structure‐properties relationships in these complex nanomaterials. The synergy of several effects makes HENA potentially efficient and stable nano‐catalysts: the “cocktail” effect due to the interaction between the different elements can give rise to enhanced reactivity which counterbalances the low content of noble metals in the nanostructure. The variety of elements and atomic sizes generate many lattice distortions and crystalline defects that can create preferential surface reaction sites. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

chosen.technique: high-throughput DSC with in situ synchrotron XRD, supported by ab initio MD free-energy integration
chosen.conditions: under inert atmosphere with slow heating and controlled equilibrium conditions across varied high‐entropy alloy compositions
chosen.why: This move directly fills the niche by addressing the need for both accuracy and efficiency in determining melting-related thermodynamic properties. It combines well-established experimental techniques (DSC and synchrotron XRD) with state-of-the-art atomistic simulation methods to overcome limitations of earlier isolated approaches, thereby providing comprehensive, validated data across the full composition range of high‐entropy alloys.

frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) transitioning from solid to liquid phases, which inherently possess complex, multi-component disordered structures in the solid state.
frame.goal: To accurately and efficiently determine key melting properties – including melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties – across the entire family of high-entropy alloys.
frame.limitation: Existing methods and models, which work well for simpler alloys, struggle with the compositional complexity and disorder inherent in HEAs. There is uncertainty regarding the physical rationale, scalability, and validation of these approaches when applied across the diverse HEA compositional space.
constraints: The approach must be underpinned by a sound physical rationale.
It must achieve quantifiable performance metrics (e.g., within specific error margins for melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy).
The range of applicability should be clearly defined, ideally covering the entire compositional space of HEAs.
Supporting prior evidence must back the proposed method.
There needs to be a decisive validation experiment or simulation outcome that, if unmet, would rule out the approach.
regime: High-temperature conditions near the melting point where solid-to-liquid transitions occur.
Thermodynamic conditions characterizing phase transitions under equilibrium or near-equilibrium settings.
prior_attempts: Traditional calorimetry techniques (e.g., differential scanning calorimetry) that have provided useful data for simpler alloy systems but lack the efficiency and precision for HEAs.

First-principles and molecular dynamics simulations that have been applied to binary and ternary alloys, yet encounter scalability and accuracy challenges when extended to multi-principal element systems.
Empirical and semi-empirical models that have been tuned for less complex materials but fail to capture the full thermodynamic behavior of HEAs.

decision.trend: Early studies in HEAs have largely focused on high‐temperature processing and phase stability rather than a systematic determination of liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties. Initial experimental work using traditional calorimetric methods provided useful data for simpler alloys but revealed major challenges when applied to HEAs because of their compositional complexity and disorder. Subsequently, first‐principles molecular dynamics and free‐energy integration studies were successfully used for binary and ternary systems, establishing a rigorous physical basis yet failing to scale to the multi‐component HEA space. More recent research in processing routes such as selective laser melting (PMC6427779) and laser powder bed fusion (PMC9229239) has highlighted the possibility of achieving rapid, near‐equilibrium melting and solidification in HEAs; however, these efforts have not been used to extract the full set of fusion thermodynamic properties with the necessary precision or across the entire compositional range.
decision.unsolved: Accurately determining melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties in HEAs remains unsolved. Existing methods either assume simpler energy landscapes or suffer from scaling issues with compositional complexity. There is a need for an approach that not only has a sound physical rationale and strict quantitative error bounds but also is validated decisively by an experiment or simulation that would rule out the approach if it fails.
decision.lever: integrated high‐throughput differential scanning calorimetry with in situ synchrotron X‐ray diffraction, combined with validation via atomistic free‐energy integration
decision.why: This step follows the trend from traditional DSC and low‐component free‐energy simulations towards methods that capture the full complexity of HEAs. The proposed combined experiment and simulation approach employs the lever of alloy composition and high‐temperature equilibration, exactly as the niche analysis suggests, to efficiently and accurately determine melting properties. Using high‐throughput DSC with in situ XRD ensures the technique is broadly applicable across the HEA compositional range, while the key validation using ab initio MD free‐energy integration provides the decisive result needed to rule out the approach if discrepancies exceed the established error margins.
